name: dnstop
desc: Console tool to analyze DNS traffic
why: Live console view of DNS traffic on the wire; a readable door into DNS that most people never watch.

brief.what_it_is: dnstop is a console tool that analyzes DNS traffic. It is a libpcap application, similar to tcpdump, that reads packets either from a live capture device or from a tcpdump savefile. It displays live tables of DNS traffic: source IP addresses, destination IP addresses, query types, response codes, opcodes, and top, second, and third level domains. It supports both IPv4 and IPv6.
brief.why_it_exists: The page frames it as a way to "Stay on Top of Your DNS Traffic" and to help find especially undesirable DNS queries, using filters for unknown or invalid TLDs, queries whose name is already an IP address, PTR queries for RFC1918 address space, and responses with code REFUSED.
brief.how_it_works: It captures packets with libpcap, as tcpdump does, and decodes them as DNS. It aggregates what it sees into the ranked tables listed above and can restrict the display to the filtered query classes. Input is either the live capture device or a saved tcpdump capture file.
brief.install_notes: The homepage shows no install steps, commands, or configuration. Live capture needs access to the capture device, which typically means running with elevated privileges, but the page does not say so. The executable is named dnstop.
brief.standout: It is a live, ranked-table view of DNS traffic on the wire, which most people never watch. It also ships built-in filters aimed at spotting bad or suspicious DNS (invalid TLDs, IP-as-name queries, RFC1918 reverse lookups, REFUSED responses).
brief.status: Unknown. The homepage is a single page with a 2020 copyright line and no release number, changelog, or last-updated date. The scout note and brew description are the only other sources, and neither gives a date.
brief.caveats: Homepage is the only source and is thin: no README, docs, screenshots, or demo were linked from it. It is hosted on a measurement-factory.com page rather than a code repository, so licensing and source availability could not be checked from what was fetched. Its output is text tables, not a graphical interface. The brew caveats field is empty.

Stay on Top of Your DNS Traffic
To help find especially undesirable DNS queries, dnstop provides a number of filters.
dnstop can either read packets from the live capture device, or from a tcpdump savefile.
